faqs.question: What makes a proposal “virtual” rather than just online?
faqs.answer: “Online” describes where the page lives; “virtual” describes the relationship. It is the word people use when the couple met on the internet, has never shared a city, or has never been in the same room — and for them the page is the venue rather than a preview of a moment happening later.

faqs.question: Can I propose on a website if we have never met in person?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the case the format is genuinely built for. The page then has to carry the whole relationship rather than trail an in-person moment, which is why a dated plan behind the yes matters more here than the animation does.

faqs.question: Should I send the link during a video call or before it?
faqs.answer: Send it first and let them read it alone. A proposal read under observation becomes a performance, and across time zones a call scheduled for the reveal usually collides with the link arriving early anyway.

faqs.question: What if they open it in the middle of their night?
faqs.answer: Assume they will. Build the page so nothing expires, nothing needs you awake, and nothing depends on a countdown — then it still works at 3am in a different country.

faqs.question: Do I really need to password-protect a proposal page?
faqs.answer: If the link could be forwarded or opened on a shared device, yes. 38.7% of SubhSandesh creators set a password before sharing (1,961 of 5,061 pages), a platform-wide figure across all 20 page types rather than a proposal-specific one.

faqs.question: How long does it take to build one?
faqs.answer: Plan for two sittings rather than one evening. The median gap between a page's first save and its last edit on SubhSandesh is 2.4 hours, sampled on the apology dashboard template with n=1,348, not on proposals — people write these, walk away and come back to fix a line.

faqs.question: Will the page still be there in ten years?
faqs.answer: A link is only a promise that a server will still answer. Take your own screen recording or screenshots and keep them as files, so the keepsake does not depend on any company staying alive.

faqs.question: Is proposing over a link less serious than asking in person?
faqs.answer: Not when the relationship was built through the same channel. Interview research on online daters describes people becoming a couple before they ever met offline, with one participant exchanging around twenty emails a day for months — a carefully written page is that channel, not a shortcut around it.

faqs.question: What should be on the screen after they tap yes?
faqs.answer: Something dated and real: a month, a flight you have actually looked up, a plan with a number in it. For a couple with no shared calendar, a proposal that ends on confetti is a promise with no next step attached.

faqs.question: What do I put on the page if most of our photos are screenshots?
faqs.answer: Use them. A grid of video-call screenshots and chat fragments is the honest record of how this relationship was actually lived, and it reads as truer than three staged photographs from the one trip you managed.

faqs.question: Which page should I use if I am asking her to be my girlfriend, not to marry me?
faqs.answer: The “I love you” page rather than the proposal scrapbook — it asks without escalating to marriage wording you would then have to explain. It is the second most-created template on SubhSandesh at 1,173 pages, 23.2% of everything made platform-wide.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Virtual Proposal Website: When the Page Is the Room

A virtual proposal website is a single personalised page you propose on when the relationship itself has been conducted at a distance, and for that couple it is not a delivery mechanism — it is the venue. There is no restaurant afterwards, no walk home, no room to turn the lights up in. On SubhSandesh, 48.4% of shared pages are opened on a phone (27,185 of 56,152 views) and 38.7% of creators password-protect the page before sharing it (1,961 of 5,061).

Both are platform-wide figures across all 20 page types, not proposal-specific ones, because there is no proposal-specific breakdown to quote. Below: what "virtual" changes, the six things the page has to carry, which build fits which distance, and when not to send one.

## What a virtual proposal website is, and why "virtual" is not "online"

A virtual proposal website is a one-page website, built from a template and personalised with your own photographs and words, that asks one named person to marry you. It is handed over as a link, opened in a browser, and answered on the page itself. The proposal template is one of 20 page types on SubhSandesh, which has recorded 5,061 pages created since 12 March 2026.

"Online" describes where the thing lives. "Virtual" describes the relationship. It is the word people reach for when the couple met on the internet, has never lived in the same city, or in some cases has never been in the same room.

For that reader the page is not a preview of the real moment. It is the moment — a different build from a card sent ahead of a booked dinner.

## The couple this page is actually for

A proposal in one city can lean on a shared world: mutual friends, a family that has met both of you, a restaurant you both know. Couples who met online frequently have none of that, and the research on how those relationships start is unusually clear about why.

Rosenfeld, Thomas and Hausen, reporting the 2017 How Couples Meet and Stay Together survey in [*PNAS* in 2019](https://web.stanford.edu/~mrosenfe/Rosenfeld_et_al_Disintermediating_Friends.pdf), found that 89.5% of couples who met online were previously strangers, with no personal connection before they met. Introduction by a third person had fallen from 11.2% of online meetings in the 2009 survey to 3.7% in 2017, and meeting online had become the most common way heterosexual American couples met, at roughly 39% of couples formed in 2017.

Two figures, one consequence. There is usually no mutual friend who can vouch for the story and no audience who watched it happen, so the page has to do that work itself.

The direction has not reversed. [Kuperberg and colleagues, in *Demographic Research* in June 2026](https://www.demographic-research.org/articles/volume/54/37), surveyed 11,993 students at 34 US colleges between 2019 and 2024 and found the share of romantic relationship partners met online rose from 20% in 2019–2020 to 25.8% in 2020–2021, ending near 24% in the final year measured — above the pre-pandemic level rather than back at it.

## Six things the page has to carry when nothing follows it in person

Each item says what it is, why distance makes it load-bearing, how long it takes, and the mistake to avoid.

### 1. The origin story, chat window and all

The opening section, telling how you actually met: the app, the group, the comment thread, the badly typed first message. Distance makes it load-bearing because nobody else can narrate it — there is no friend who introduced you and can tell it later.

Fifteen minutes. The mistake is being embarrassed by the beginning and starting the story at the first video call.

### 2. Proof that you know their ordinary day

Two or three lines about their commute, their shift, the thing they complain about every Thursday. The standing suspicion about a relationship at a distance is that you are in love with an image, and specific, unglamorous detail is the strongest evidence against it.

Ten minutes. The mistake is listing what you love about them instead of what you know about them.

### 3. A question they can answer alone, in their own hour

One screen, one sentence, with the two buttons under it. Across time zones you do not get to choose the minute they read it, so the page has to work at 6am and at midnight with you asleep.

One minute to write. The mistake is booking a video call for the reveal and letting the link arrive first.

### 4. Something dated and real behind the yes

The screen after the answer: a month, a flight you have actually looked up, a plan with a number in it. Without a shared calendar the proposal is otherwise a promise with no next step attached to it.

Ten minutes. The mistake is ending on confetti.

### 5. A lock, because the link is the only private room you have

A password set before the link is shared. A couple in one city can close a door; a couple in two cities has only a URL, and a URL travels. 38.7% of SubhSandesh creators set one before sharing, platform-wide across all 20 page types.

Thirty seconds. The mistake is setting it afterwards, once the link has already been forwarded.

### 6. A copy that outlives the website

A screen recording or a set of screenshots you take yourself and keep as files. Pages like this get reopened rather than read once — the platform-wide average is 11.1 views per created page — and a link is a promise that a server will still answer in ten years.

Two minutes. The mistake is assuming a web address is permanent.

SubhSandesh's [Will You Marry Me proposal scrapbook](/proposal) is built to that shape: your story in order, ending in a YES button that grows every time they dodge it. One platform-wide number worth knowing before you start — 91.2% of pages begun on the platform are published and shared (4,615 of 5,061), so the build is short enough that people finish it.

## Which build fits which kind of distance

The table sorts by how the relationship was formed rather than by feature, because that is what changes the job. The last column carries a distinct SubhSandesh figure, each platform-wide across 20 page types.

| Your situation | What the page has to carry | Closest build | First-party figure to weigh |
|---|---|---|---|
| Same city, seeing each other weekly | Almost nothing; say it out loud instead | None — the format is wrong here | 48.4% of views are on a phone, and so is a text message |
| Met in person, now two cities | The journey and the date it ends | [Train Ticket](/train-ticket) | 11.1 average views per page — it gets reread |
| Met online, have since met in person | The origin story, told without apology | [Proposal scrapbook](/proposal) | 38.7% of creators lock the page before sharing |
| Met online, never met in person | The whole relationship, plus a dated plan | Proposal scrapbook, locked | 91.2% of started pages are published and shared |

The bottom two rows are what this page exists for; the fourth cannot lean on a single memory that happened in a room.

## Timing, time zones, and building it across two sittings

You do not control when a link is opened, so build as though you will not be there. No countdown that expires, no instruction to open it at 8pm, no surprise that depends on you being awake in another time zone.

Give yourself two sittings. On SubhSandesh the median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 2.4 hours, sampled on the apology dashboard template with n=1,348 rather than on proposals, which says people write these, walk away, and come back to fix one line.

That instinct fits the material, which is what the relationship was built from. In interviews with online daters in Germany and Switzerland, [Dröge and Voirol reported in the *Journal of Family Research* in 2011](https://ubp.uni-bamberg.de/jfr/index.php/jfr/article/view/200) that people can "become a couple before they actually met outside the Internet" — one participant exchanged around twenty emails a day for months with a partner abroad before any meeting. A page written carefully is not a lesser way of asking. It is the channel that carried everything else.

## When a virtual proposal website is the wrong choice

**You are in the same city.** Say it out loud. A link handed to someone you will see on Saturday turns a moment into an errand, and the page's best property — that it crosses a distance — is wasted.

**You are in love with an image.** The same interviews carry the warning. One participant later described her online relationship as a "huge bubble", adding that it was "strange how one can be obsessed with an image of somebody". A well-made page amplifies an image, which is exactly the wrong thing to do if you have never heard this person at a bad moment.

**The obstacle is a milestone, not a question.** [Zerui Tian's 2026 SocArXiv preprint](https://osf.io/preprints/socarxiv/25k8b) — not peer-reviewed — analysing Generations and Gender Survey data across nine European countries reports that unions formed through online dating were associated less with poorer relationship quality than with how those unions get converted into marriage and shared childbearing. Read plainly: the friction for couples who met online tends to sit at the formal steps rather than in the relationship, and no page clears a visa queue or a conversation with a parent.

**It is not a marriage proposal.** If the question is "will you be my girlfriend", the ["I love you" page](/love-gf) is the honest fit — it asks without escalating, and it was the second most-created template on the platform at 1,173 pages, 23.2% of everything made.

## Sources

- Rosenfeld, Thomas & Hausen, ["Disintermediating your friends: How online dating in the United States displaces other ways of meeting"](https://web.stanford.edu/~mrosenfe/Rosenfeld_et_al_Disintermediating_Friends.pdf), *PNAS* 116(36), 2019 — open author copy.
- Kuperberg, Daniels, Curington & Lundquist, ["Partnering in turbulent times"](https://www.demographic-research.org/articles/volume/54/37), *Demographic Research* 54(37), 10 June 2026.
- Dröge & Voirol, ["Online dating: The tensions between romantic love and economic rationalization"](https://ubp.uni-bamberg.de/jfr/index.php/jfr/article/view/200), *Journal of Family Research* 23(3), 2011.
- Tian, ["Love at First Swipe: Online Dating and Relationship Outcomes in Europe"](https://osf.io/preprints/socarxiv/25k8b), SocArXiv, 15 August 2026 — a preprint, not peer-reviewed.

SubhSandesh figures are first-party, measured 2026-09-23, platform-wide across 20 page types except the 2.4-hour edit gap, sampled on the apology dashboard template.

structuralLimitations: No proposal-specific first-party data exists: a read-only probe of the proposalpages collection is refused by this machine's production-read policy. Every SubhSandesh figure in the post is labelled in body prose as platform-wide across all 20 page types, or as sampled on the named template (the 2.4-hour edit gap, /apology-dashboard, n=1,348). No figure is attributed to proposal pages.
The pricing block in content/facts.md is empty for the third batch running, so the post states and implies no price, no free tier and no paid tier anywhere.

Phase 1 is thin and partly uncomparable to the target market. One US-served WebSearch was run on 2026-09-23 (WebSearch is US-only from this machine) and the audience is India; the 11 India-served SERPs in content/keywords/2026-09-16-propose-100/serps.md were measured 2026-09-16 and do not cover this keyword. No ranking page was fetched, so the post makes no claim about what competitors cover, omit or rank for, and no position is described as current.

One of the four sources (Tian 2026, SocArXiv) is a preprint that has not been peer-reviewed, and only its abstract was read via the OSF API. Both facts are stated in the body prose and in the on-page sources list.

Cacioppo et al. (2013, PNAS) is the most directly relevant paper on how online-initiated marriages fare and was deliberately not cited: the only readable copies sit on pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, which is at the 3-post domain cap for this batch, and on ResearchGate, which is not citable.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page in this cluster written for the reader whose relationship was formed online rather than merely delivered online, and the only one that sorts the build by how the couple met instead of by file format, link mechanics or template slot. The citation case is genuinely strong — four open-access sources on relationship formation online, three peer-reviewed and read in full, next to first-party page data no competitor can publish. What it cannot overcome: an unmeasured India-served SERP for this exact keyword, a domain far below the engagement-ring retailers and builder sites that hold this space, and a band of 300–1,000 estimated monthly searches, which means even a good position returns modest traffic. Ranking takes months and this post does not predict one.
